Gracias, Hector. I thank Ambassador Hernandez for his statement. And I'll now turn to our panel of distinguished speakers. First, I'd like to pass the floor to Ms. Elise Moschini, who is the permanent observer of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent to the UN. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I would like first to thank Denmark, Spain, and New Zealand for convening this meeting and bringing urgently needed attention to the protection of health care in armed conflict. Ten years ago, the Security Council Resolution 2286 was adopted in response to intolerable attacks, threats, obstruction affecting medical care in conflict. It reaffirmed the protection owed to the wounded and sick, medical personnel, transports, and facilities, and called for the effective military doctrine and practice, domestic normative frameworks, and accountability for ensuring safe access to medical care. Ten years later, violence affecting medical facilities, transport, and personnel has continued. And in many contexts, harm this resolution sought to prevent has intensified. Put simply, the unacceptable situation that led the Council to act 10 years ago is even worse today. Ambulances held at checkpoints, attacked during evacuations, patients injured or killed while receiving treatment. Medical staff brutally targeted. Clinics without medicines, operating rooms without anaesthetics. Families walking for days to reach safe medical care after fleeing violence. These are the conditions the International Committee of the Red Cross sees in our operations today. It must be said here, when healthcare is no longer safe, it is a clear warning sign that the rules and norms intended to limit the harm of war are breaking down. While many dangers identified in resolution 2286 remain, we also better understand today how much healthcare depends on other essential services. Hospitals do not function in isolation. Damage to electrical grids, water systems, fuel supplies, transport routes, or communications networks can disable intensive care units, interrupt surgery, compromise cold chains, and prevent ambulances from reaching the wounded and sick. This is particularly visible in populated urban settings where civilians, hospitals, and essential services are concentrated. A single strike can cut power, block roads, damage water systems, and overwhelm nearby hospitals at the same time. When these other systems are degraded by hostilities, healthcare systems are compromised. New risks are also emerging. The use of AI-enabled systems in military operations may influence targeting and operational decisions. But this must not undermine the protection owed to civilians, medical personnel, and facilities. These tools must support, not replace, informed human judgment where lives are at stake. Cyber operations must not target or unduly disrupt hospital systems and patient data. IHL applies regardless of the means or method of warfare. New technologies do not create legal vacuums. International humanitarian law provides robust protections for healthcare and the systems that sustain it. Full implementation of these obligations is essential and urgent. The ICRC's recommendations to the UN Security Council and to all states are practical. First, protection of healthcare must begin before conflict erupts and be integrated throughout military operations in doctrine, planning, targeting procedures, rules of engagement, training, and command responsibility. Hospital locations must be systematically identified and their protection reflected in targeting decisions. Civilian harm mitigation measures must be in place from the outset. This requires protecting the systems that sustain healthcare. Protection of healthcare cannot be improvised once hostilities begin. Second, medical care must remain impartial and protected. Patients must be treated based on medical need alone. Medical personnel must be able to work in accordance with medical ethics. Health services must never become instruments of military strategy, pressure, or punishment. Access to healthcare must also be safeguarded, including through rapid and unimpeded passage of medical personnel, ambulances, and essential supplies. Across our operations, we see the extraordinary commitment of health workers who continue to provide care under extremely difficult and often dangerous conditions. Their determination in this vital work represents a lifeline of hope for those caught in war's devastation, but it cannot compensate for a failure of protection. We appreciate the attention given to protecting healthcare in armed conflict, as demonstrated through the important engagement of States today, and through events including the Greentree Retreat on Renewing Commitment to Protection of Healthcare in Armed Conflict under IHL, which was held in March, as well as further events planned for Protection of Civilians Week and around the anniversary of the adoption of Resolution 2286. We call for States to deliver on this momentum. As highlighted in the joint call issued just two days ago by the ICRC President, the Director General of the World Health Organization, and the International President of Medecins Sans Frontieres, the recommendations of the UN's Secretary General that followed Resolution 2286 remain clear and actionable roadmap for states. We stand ready with our presence in conflict settings, medical expertise, and operational capacity to support states in implementing these critical measures. We also encourage states to join and contribute to the aims of the global initiative to galvanize political commitment to international humanitarian law. The dedicated work stream on the meaningful protection of hospitals in armed conflict, co-chaired by Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain, and Uruguay, is identifying practical ways to strengthen implementation based on state practices. To conclude, renewed commitment and action are required by all states. Places of healing must remain sanctuaries, especially in war's darkest moments. Because when a hospital is bombed, a doctor is killed, or an ambulance evacuating a patient is targeted, it is a direct attack on the very fabric of our shared humanity. We must act to uphold humanitarian war. Thank you.

Excellencies, colleagues, I would like to thank Denmark, Spain, and New Zealand for convening this meeting. We heard it already. Ten years ago, this council unanimously adopted resolution 2286 in response to an intolerable reality. Hospitals bombed, ambulances attacked, Patients killed in their beds. Medical workers ended for carrying their duty. The resolution was born of outrage at the systematic targeting of healthcare in Syria and at the bombing and destruction of MSF's trauma center in Kunduz. It carried a promise to match that outrage, that such attack would never be accepted as a normal feature of war and that when the deed occur, states would take responsibility for stopping them and ensuring there were consequences. Ten years on, that promise lies in ruins. What shocked the conscience in 2016 now too often passes without the bare minimum of condemnation, let alone consequence. It has become routine, as if attacking healthcare were an acceptable cost of war, and the principle meant to prevent it something to be set aside when inconvenient. In conflict after conflict, we are observing the unmaking of protection you once pledged to defend. In Gaza, the scale and intensity of attacks on healthcare over the past two and a half years have been staggering. As part of a broader assault on the Gaza civilian population, the Israeli armed forces have besieged, ratted, and gutted hospitals. They have killed displaced, and detained medical staff, many of whom still languish in jails. Since October 2023, 15 of our MSF colleagues have been killed. Today, amid a so-called ceasefire, and when humanitarian aid is meant to be flowing freely into the Strip, MSF teams in Gaza are being prevented from restocking essential supplies. Their ability to care for their patients is being stripped away. What makes Gaza distinct is not only the scale of the assault on the health system, it is the way the law itself is being bent to justify it. Israeli forces have repeatedly invoked loss of protection under IHL, the claim that hospitals had been used for military purposes and therefore forfeited their protected status, claims almost never independently verified. But that special protection is not lost by mere allegation. It can only be set aside under strict conditions, after a warning has been issued and ignored, and the specific part of the facility qualifies as a military objective, and only when attacks comply with the principles of proportionality and precaution, which remain binding at all times. Based on MSF experience across conflict, we see no realistic circumstances in which the destruction of a functioning hospital could be lawful, let alone morally justifiable. The military gain is marginal and short-lived. The harm to civilians is predictable and lasting. What we have seen in the expensive use of the loss of protection argument is the exception swallowing the rule. Suspicion replaces evidence. Protection granted by default is treated as something hospitals must prove they still deserve. In South Sudan, the pattern of attacks has been different, but the consequence is no less devastating. In April 2025, armed men stormed our hospital in Ulang, looted the facility and forced more than 100 patients to flee in the middle of treatment. Weeks later, in Old Fangak, government forces bombed the MSF hospital, despite its location having been communicated to all parties to the conflict. It was the only hospital serving more than 100,000 people. In February of this year, in Lankian, government's forces struck again, bombing the hospital's compound and destroying critical medical supplies in the only secondary-level facility serving nearly 250,000 people. What followed was looting and deliberate destruction, nothing left to sustain services. As a result of these attacks, entire communities have been cut off from medical care for trauma, for childbirth, for condition caused or compounded by conflict. The impact of individual attacks reverberates well beyond the moment. Again, when hospitals are struck, the consequences are immediate, long-lasting, and entirely predictable. In many areas, care does not adapt and shift. It disappears. And those launching these attacks know exactly what deprivation they are inflicting. Over the past 10 years, similar attacks have been carried out across practically every major conflict. From Syria to Sudan, from Ukraine to Afghanistan, from Ethiopia to Lebanon. Violations have piled up while Resolution 2286 is invoked in annual debates, commemorated in side events, but left undefended where it matters most. Some States have directly contributed to this erosion, and in many cases the perpetrators are States themselves. Others have enabled it through silence, selectivity or political cover. Attacks on healthcare are today a standard feature of war. That normalization was not inevitable. It was permitted, incident by incident, year after year, under your watch as custodians of this resolution. If resolution 2286 is to retain any meaning, it cannot remain a ritual invocation while hospitals burn. It must become the basis of a more robust protective framework. That responsibility rests here, with this Council, but it does not stop here. It extends to every member state. Each of you has an obligation not only to comply with IHL, but to ensure respect for it. That means adopting military practices that protect healthcare, investigating violation, and making the findings public, and holding those responsible to account. It also means looking outward. States that provide military support, intelligence, or political backing to parties to conflicts cannot treat attacks on healthcare as a secondary concern. That support must be conditioned on respect for IHL. An actionable blueprint already exists. Through the Global Initiative Workstream on the Protection of Hospitals, over 100 states are already working to advance practical measures to protect medical facilities in conflict, measures grounded in operational reality and consistent with the existing legal framework. They show how wars can be waged while still protecting hospitals through responsible choices in targeting and the deliberate preservation of essential services. They are not aspirational standards. They represent the bare minimum required, and they are equally applicable to the protection of medical workers and transport. What is needed now is implementation in good faith. As for this Council, it has not meaningfully attempted to enforce Resolution 2286. It has failed to use the tools already at its disposal to track and respond to these attacks. That must change. The Council should address the protection of health care regularly through briefings, reporting, and concrete follow-up. Where serious violations occur, it should support independent investigation and accountability mechanisms. The Secretary-General has a role to play as well. Reporting must go beyond general trends mentioned in the annual Protection of Civilians report. It should identify patterns, name perpetrators, and trigger Council action when healthcare is attacked or obstructed. Today's discussion centers in part on emerging threats to the medical mission, the risk posed by AI-driven targeting systems, by the proliferation of drones, and by the increasing automation of warfare. These development matters. We already are seeing their effects in our wards. But we should be clear about where the real danger lies here. It's not only in the weapons being developed. It is in the responsibility you are failing to uphold. If there is no will to stop the bombing of our hospitals, the targeting of our colleagues, and the killing of our patients today, what chance do we stand when warfare becomes faster, more automated, and further removed from human judgment? For our patients trapped in conflict and for our colleagues who continue risking their lives to provide care under fire, what happens next will be shaped by the action you take, or those you choose not to. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Moe, for that very compelling briefing. And I now pass the floor to the Professor Len Rubenstein from Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who's also the representative of Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition. The floor is yours, sir.

Ambassador Zelasny, Hernandez, Schwager, distinguished members of the Security Council and colleagues. I thank Denmark, Spain, and New Zealand for convening this session and for the opportunity to address the catastrophic violence inflicted on health care in war and what can be done to reverse the trend. Resolution 2286 provided a roadmap for member states to curb violence against health care in armed conflict and to end impunity for it. But states have not fulfilled their commitments. The resolution's history is of inaction, not implementation, of impunity, not accountability. I have investigated violence against healthcare in war for more than 25 years and am past chair of the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition. Since 2014, the coalition has reported annually on the bombing, shelling, and looting of hospitals and ambulances the arrests, detention, kidnapping, and killing of health workers. The data we've collected shows that today, violence against health care is far more pervasive and destructive than it was 10 years ago when the resolution was adopted. From 20 to 24, the number of incidents nearly tripled, led by assaults in Gaza, Lebanon, Myanmar, Sudan, and Ukraine. Coalition member Insecurity Insight just released data showing 18,000 incidents over the 10 years since the resolution, amounting to almost five incidents every single day over the decade, including 4,700 that damaged or destroyed health facilities and more than 3,800 health workers killed. Other trends are also going in the wrong direction. State militaries have replaced non-state armed groups as the main perpetrators of attacks. Military forces are increasingly employing explosive weapons, even against maternity services, as Russia has done in Ukraine more than 100 times. Combatants have targeted health facilities with drones more than 1,000 times. In Sudan, doctors perform surgery in small shipping containers covered by sand and rocks to escape the drones launched by them by the rapid support forces. Grotesque multiple strikes that target rescuers are also common in this day and age. In addition to that, Militaries act with contempt for international humanitarian law or reinterpret it to undermine its protective provisions and purposes. In Gaza and Lebanon, Israel routinely justifies attacks on hospitals by claiming that they're used to commit acts harmful to the enemy. But in almost all cases, it offers scant or no evidence of military use. and entirely ignores strict legal requirements of proportionality and precaution to avoid the attacks altogether, limit their impact, protect patients and medical personnel, and preserve healthcare for communities going forward. This violence undermines the right to health of populations already suffering in war. Extensive research has shown that patients die not only in the explosions, but from the degradation of health systems capacity to provide desperately needed care for chronic and infectious disease, safe childbirth, and traumatic injuries. Health workers, as well as patients, suffer long-lasting psychological trauma as well. In the face of these horrors, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, UN Commissions of Inquiry, and the Special Representative on Armed Conflict, are doing their part to document attacks, call out perpetrators, and demand accountability. The World Health Organization has committed to improve its surveillance system for attacks on healthcare. The International Committee of the Red Cross has launched an initiative to galvanize political commitment to international humanitarian law. But states have largely abdicated their responsibilities They rarely investigate and hold their own forces to account. They provide weapons and other military aid to forces that commit war crimes against healthcare. They rarely employ diplomatic, economic, and prosecutorial tools to impose consequences on perpetrators. That must change. To start, The Council must hold Member States accountable to their own commitment in 2286 by requiring annual reporting on implementation of the resolution. It should also require the Secretary-General to inform the Council more regularly and provide in-depth reports on conflicts of particular concerns, as well as global trends, including efforts to undermine the law. And member states need to act beyond the council. As proposed in a report by the World Health Organization and the World Innovation Summit on Health, member states truly committed to protection of healthcare in conflict should join civil society and UN agencies in a new alliance to collaborate in exerting diplomatic, economic, and other sources of leverage to stop the violence. The alliance can demand proper application of the law. It can coordinate action to restrict arms sales and other forms of military support to perpetrators of attacks. It can press for investigations and prosecutions by international regional courts, which are still largely absent, and support universal jurisdiction. And it can expand and coordinate monitoring. There are excellent models for such alliances, for collaboration and joint action. These include the campaign to ban landmines, campaigns on safe schools in conflict, among others. Impunity is a political choice. In the name of humanity and justice, joint, coordinated, and assertive action can finally realize the unfulfilled promise of Resolution 2286 and end the scourge of violence against healthcare in war. Thank you.

And I thank Professor Rubenstein for his briefing. I now turn to the last briefer of this panel, Professor Nas Mudirzade, who is the director of Harvard Law School's Program on International Law and Armed Conflict. You have the floor.

Thank you so much. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I join my co-panelists in expressing my gratitude to Denmark, Spain, and New Zealand for convening this meeting and to the earlier briefers for underscoring the urgency of protecting the medical mission. A familiar account, and one that we have crucially heard about today, is that medical care is endangered when hospitals are bombed, ambulances are struck, healthcare workers are detained, or the wounded and sick are denied care. That account remains true, but it captures only part of the story. Today, risks also arise through digital infrastructure and decision processes that shape the use of force and other military operations. Cyber operations can, for example, make hospital networks unusable, impair medical equipment, or compromise patient data. Apart from cyber attacks, artificial intelligence decision support systems are increasingly being integrated into armed conflicts. An AI DSS refers to a system that uses machine learning or other algorithmic techniques to analyze information and present recommendations, assessments, or predictions to a human decision maker. In certain armed conflicts, AI decision support systems are being used to assist with aspects related to target identification, threat assessment, intelligence analysis, or the prioritization of objects for attack or protection. Partly by affecting what information is elevated, how uncertainty is presented, and how quickly people are asked to make decisions, these systems may introduce new risks for how humans carry out legal obligations. These risks may be less visible than missile strikes, but ultimately, they can be just as consequential for the wounded and sick. Against that background, I would therefore wish to offer three reflections. First, in the context of a growing number of contemporary armed conflicts, humans are deciding to develop and use AI decision support systems and cyber technologies. A key concern here is whether in doing so, those humans will choose to retain the conditions needed to uphold IHL obligations in good faith. All militaries operate under time pressure and with incomplete information. In the cyber context, those realities do not diminish obligations related to respecting and protecting the medical mission. A hospital today is not just a building, but also an information system. If records are inaccessible, a doctor may not know whether a child can receive a transfusion. If the network fails, a surgeon may lose the image that shows where the shrapnel sits. And if communications are disrupted, an ambulance may circle in the dark while a wounded person waits, alive for now, but potentially not for long. AI-enabled decision support systems raise related issues. Such systems may offer advantages in managing large volumes of information. but when configured for rapid processing or probabilistic assessment, their outputs typically remain statistical inferences, not legal determinations. These systems may help humans to organize information, but they cannot themselves understand the scope of an IHL obligation or carry it out in good faith. Several concerns may arise in connection with such systems. In the context of target identification or threat assessment, an AIDSS may not make clear how it generated an output, which can hinder a commander's ability to verify the protected status of medical personnel, units, and transports. In intelligence analysis or the prioritization of objects for attack or protection, systems may fail to adequately detect or appropriately weight indicators of exclusive medical use, thereby risking that such objects are not accorded the caution and protection they require. Some systems may also compress complex contextual judgments, such as the risk of incidental harm to medical personnel, into simplified scores that do not reflect their full legal significance. In these settings, reliance on AI DSS may encourage undue deference to system outputs rather than the deliberate exercise of judgment needed to ensure respect for and protection of the medical mission. Further, bias remains a significant concern, including where it may lead to the under-recognition of protected medical activities or to erroneous classifications that expose medical personnel or facilities to attack or other forms of impermissible interference. Second, this is a moment for states and other stakeholders to exercise agency. Decisions about how to regulate the role of AI and cyber operations in armed conflict, and I really wish to underscore this point, do not rest only with actors developing and deploying these technologies. To the contrary, all states are legally empowered to shape what is understood as lawful and what is understood as unacceptable. They can clarify that AI-enabled systems must not displace human cognitive agency, judgment, and responsibility. They can require sufficient human supervision, attentive to testing, verification, and preset limits, as well as legal reviews of new capabilities. And they can develop doctrine and integrate it into training. They can also articulate that cyber operations must not unduly interfere with protective medical services. The ICT's work stream of the global initiative to galvanize political support for IHL, for example, offers an existing forum for developing and expressing those latter considerations. Excellencies, my third and final reflection is that the question is not whether technology will shape armed conflict and the protection of civilians. It always has and it always will. The question I would like to invite you to consider is whether the normative commitments underpinning IHL will be carried forward with legal clarity and political courage in a period marked by increasingly rapid and extensive reliance on AI and other digital infrastructures. Thank you.

Madam President, allow me to begin by expressing gratitude to the co-organizers, Denmark, Spain and New Zealand, for convening this meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of the adoption of resolution 2286 of the Security Council. We come to this 10th anniversary at a breaking point. In 2025, those killed in attacks against medical missions were double the number recorded in 2024. They reached a spine-chilling total of 1,981 people dead. Today, we are seeing an average of 4.3 such attacks every day. This demonstrates that violence against personnel who tirelessly work to save lives in the midst of war is an increasing trend. and one which persists in many current conflicts. These acts not only strip people of life-saving care, they also undermine irreversibly healthcare systems and compel mass displacement. The map of this horror is vast. The occupied Palestinian territory, for example, reported the highest number of incidents ever between 2024 and 2025, according to the WHO's surveillance system for attacks on healthcare. We also know that today, none of the 36 hospitals in Gaza is fully functional. There, health personnel operate in bitterly difficult, extreme conditions, facing not only the direct risk of attacks, but also the strain resulting from the collapse of healthcare infrastructure and the critical shortage of both inputs and personnel. Situations in Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Lebanon, and Syria reinforce this alarming trend. We must be clear, attacking a hospital or a member of a medical mission is not only a flagrant violation of IHL, it is an attack against the civilian population in its entirety. The problem is not a lack of norms, rather it is persistent impunity. To close this gap, we must fully discharge the mandate of resolution 2286, and we must strive to strengthen legal measures which guarantee the unfettered provision of healthcare services. We must here recall that attacks against healthcare infrastructure may constitute war crimes. For as long as there are no tangible consequences for the perpetrators, particularly when 81% of these incidents can be attributed to state actors, our commitments will continue to fall short. Moreover, effective justice is the only real guarantee for the protection of local personnel, who tragically account for 98% of victims. We urge States to heed the recommendations of the Secretary-General and to implement the Geneva Conventions together with their Additional Protocols, this without exception. Madam President, Technology must be our ally in documenting cases and in ensuring that evidence is preserved for future legal proceedings. At the same time, we must mitigate emerging risks. Cyber attacks on hospitals and the use of artificial intelligence in the selection of targets cannot be grey areas which dilute human responsibility. criminal liability must always lie with the human judgment that must uphold obligations of distinction and proportionality. With this in mind, integrating the protection of medical missions into military doctrines, as well as into training and operational planning, remains a legitimate recommendation, all the more so in light of the use of emerging technologies for military purposes. Moreover, Restrictions on humanitarian access and operational constraints documented by the WHO, including blockades preventing the entry of medical supplies and obstacles to high-risk medical missions, demonstrate that the protection of health care personnel cannot be decoupled from guaranteeing safe and sustainable conditions for the provision of health care services on the ground. To conclude, I do wish to underscore that as we look to the next decade, this Council must lead the way in terms of decrying these acts and ensuring legal consequences. Protecting the medical mission is the last vestige of humanity. The time has come to guarantee that no doctor or member of a medical mission has to choose between saving a life and losing their own. due to a lack of justice and the persistence of impunity. I would also like to thank those who shared their views with us, the ICRC, Medecins Sans Frontieres, Doctors Without Borders, the SHCC, and the University of Harvard. We have taken note of your reports duly with respect to international humanitarian law, the humanitarian situation, and vis-a-vis the developments, and I put quotes here, the techniques of war and the importance attributed to the to tackling the matter that we are dealing with in the light of technological progress. Madam President, we applaud the work that is being done on the ground by humanitarian organizations. be they part of the United Nations system, multilateral system, or civil society. And we pay tribute to all healthcare personnel in conflict, particularly those individuals who have lost their lives as they delivered upon their duties when they should have been protected.
